promptText: What is the key behavioral difference between debounce and throttle?
options: Debounce fires once after calls stop for a wait period; throttle guarantees the function runs at most once per fixed interval even during continuous activity
They are functionally identical; only the implementation differs
Throttle waits for silence before firing; debounce fires on a fixed schedule
Debounce only works with async functions, throttle only works with sync functions
explanation: Debounce collapses a burst of calls into a single call after activity settles (good for search-as-you-type); throttle enforces a steady maximum rate during continuous activity (good for scroll/mousemove handlers).

promptText: Why is `requestAnimationFrame` generally preferred over `setTimeout(fn, 16)` for animations?
options: requestAnimationFrame runs on a separate thread from the main JS thread
requestAnimationFrame is synced to the browser's actual repaint cycle and automatically pauses in background tabs, while setTimeout drifts and keeps firing (throttled) even when the tab is hidden
setTimeout cannot accept a callback function, only a string of code
requestAnimationFrame ignores the refresh rate and always fires at exactly 60fps
explanation: rAF callbacks fire right before the next repaint, adapting to the display's actual refresh rate and pausing automatically when the tab is backgrounded, unlike setTimeout which has no awareness of the paint cycle and keeps running (throttled) in hidden tabs.

promptText: When a fetch request is cancelled via `controller.abort()`, what happens to the fetch promise, and how should calling code handle it?
options: The promise resolves normally with an empty response body
The promise rejects with an error named "AbortError", which the calling code should explicitly check for and treat as an expected cancellation, not a real failure
The promise never settles at all
The abort silently cancels the request with no observable effect on the promise
explanation: An aborted fetch rejects with a DOMException named AbortError; well-written code checks err.name === "AbortError" and treats it as an intentional cancellation rather than surfacing it as a genuine failure to the user.

options: They are aliases for the same behavior

Promise.race settles on whichever promise settles first, fulfilled or rejected; Promise.any settles as soon as the first promise fulfills, and only rejects (with an AggregateError) if every promise rejects
Promise.any always waits for all promises regardless of outcome
Promise.race only works with two promises; Promise.any works with any number
explanation: Promise.race is indifferent to success/failure — first to settle wins either way. Promise.any is optimistic — it ignores failures until literally everything has failed, at which point it rejects with an AggregateError collecting every reason.

promptText: What is the defining property of WeakMap keys compared to Map keys?
options: WeakMap keys can be any primitive value, unlike Map
WeakMap keys are held weakly — if nothing else references the key object, it (and its entry) becomes eligible for garbage collection, unlike a Map's strong references
WeakMap keys are always strings internally
WeakMap entries expire automatically after a fixed timeout
explanation: A WeakMap's keys must be objects and are held weakly, meaning the presence of a key in the WeakMap does not prevent that object from being garbage collected once nothing else references it — a Map would keep the key (and thus the object) alive indefinitely.

promptText: In Node.js, how does `process.nextTick()` compare in priority to a resolved Promise's `.then()` callback?
options: process.nextTick runs at a lower priority and always runs after all promise microtasks
process.nextTick's queue is drained before the promise microtask queue — it's a separate, even higher-priority queue than standard microtasks
They are exactly the same queue with no ordering difference
process.nextTick is deprecated and behaves identically to setTimeout(fn, 0)
explanation: process.nextTick queues callbacks on a Node-specific queue that is fully drained — including any nextTicks scheduled during that draining — before the standard promise microtask queue gets a turn, making it a distinct, higher-priority mechanism.

promptText: Three independent 300ms API calls are awaited one after another inside an async function, taking ~900ms total. What is the correct fix to make them run in ~300ms, and why does it work?
options: Wrap each call in its own separate async function — this alone parallelizes them

Start all three promises first (without awaiting immediately) or pass them to Promise.all, so their underlying work begins concurrently instead of each one waiting for the previous to finish before even starting
Add `await` before each call plus a manual setTimeout(0) between them
Sequential awaiting is actually the fastest option; 900ms is unavoidable for independent calls
explanation: await pauses the function at each line, so writing awaits back-to-back only starts the next call after the previous one resolves. Kicking off all three calls first (or using Promise.all) lets their underlying async work run concurrently, since starting the promise begins the operation immediately regardless of when you await it.

promptText: Why does `items.forEach(async (item) => { await save(item); }); console.log("done");` log "done" before any items have actually finished saving?
options: forEach ignores the promise returned by its async callback entirely — it never awaits it, so it fires all the callbacks and moves on immediately regardless of how long they take
console.log is always scheduled as a microtask, running before any awaited code
save() is synchronous by definition, so this code has a different bug
forEach only supports synchronous callbacks and would throw a TypeError here
explanation: Array.prototype.forEach has no way to wait for the promises its callbacks return — it just invokes each callback and moves to the next, so the surrounding code continues immediately. The fix is a for...of loop with await (sequential) or Promise.all(items.map(...)) (parallel).

promptText: What is the precise distinction between currying and partial application?
options: They are identical techniques with different names in different languages

Currying transforms a function of N arguments into N nested unary functions called one at a time (f(a)(b)(c)); partial application fixes some arguments now and returns a function that still takes the remaining arguments as a group
Partial application only works with arrow functions; currying only works with regular functions
Currying can only be applied to functions with exactly two parameters
explanation: Currying strictly hands arguments one at a time through a chain of unary functions, while partial application (often via bind or a closure) pre-fills some arguments and returns a function that still accepts the rest together, not necessarily one at a time.

promptText: Why does resolving a promise with a custom "thenable" object (one with a .then method but not a real Promise) cost at least one extra microtask tick compared to resolving with a plain value?
options: Thenables are always processed as macrotasks instead of microtasks

The engine must call the thenable's own .then() method and wait for it to invoke its callback, rather than immediately treating the value as settled — that indirection adds an additional round trip through the microtask queue
Thenables are converted to strings before resolution, which takes extra time
This is a myth; there is no timing difference in the spec
explanation: When a thenable is passed to Promise.resolve() (or returned from a .then callback), the engine can't assume it's already spec-compliant — it must call the thenable's .then and wait for it to call back, which requires at least one more microtask tick than settling with an ordinary value directly.

promptText: Why is adding random jitter to an exponential backoff retry strategy important, beyond just increasing the delay each attempt?
options: Jitter makes each individual retry succeed with higher probability

Without jitter, many clients that failed at the same moment (e.g. after a brief outage) would retry in perfect unison, creating a synchronized "thundering herd" that can re-trigger the very outage they're recovering from
Jitter is required by the Fetch API specification for all retried requests
Jitter reduces the total number of retry attempts needed
explanation: Pure exponential backoff without randomness means a fleet of clients that failed simultaneously will all retry at the same computed delays, hammering the server in synchronized waves; jitter spreads those retries out over time to avoid that thundering-herd effect.

promptText: Before `let` existed, how did engineers fix the classic bug where `for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) { setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 10); }` logged the same final value three times?
options: There was no fix available before ES6; the bug was considered unavoidable
Wrap the timeout call in an IIFE that takes the current value of i as its own parameter, creating a fresh, private scope per iteration that captures that iteration's value
Replace setTimeout with setInterval, which has different closure semantics
Declare i three separate times using var, once per expected callback
explanation: An IIFE invoked immediately with the current i as an argument creates a new function scope per iteration, and that scope's own parameter (not the shared loop variable) is what each timeout's closure captures — exactly the effect let later provided natively.

promptText: Consider: `console.log(1); setTimeout(() => console.log(2), 0); async function run(){ console.log(3); await null; console.log(4); } run(); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(5)); console.log(6);` What is the output order?
explanation: Synchronous code runs first: 1, then run() executes synchronously up to its first await (3), then 6. run()'s await schedules continuation 4 as a microtask before the standalone .then() line even executes, so it's queued first; then 5's .then() is queued. Microtasks drain in that order (4 then 5), and finally the macrotask 2 runs last.

promptText: Why can't Vue 2's Object.defineProperty-based reactivity detect a newly added property on a reactive object (`data.b = 2` after initialization), while Vue 3's Proxy-based reactivity can?
options: Object.defineProperty is fundamentally slower, not fundamentally different in capability

Object.defineProperty must be applied per-property, upfront, at initialization time — it cannot retroactively intercept a property that didn't exist yet; a Proxy intercepts at the object level, so any property access — including ones added afterward — passes through the same trap automatically
Vue 2 doesn't support adding properties to objects at all
Proxy objects can only be created for arrays, not general objects
explanation: Vue 2's approach walks every existing property once and wraps each with a getter/setter, so anything added later was never wrapped and is invisible to the reactivity system (requiring Vue.set as a workaround). A Proxy wraps the whole object, so its get/set/deleteProperty traps fire for any key — old or new — with no special-casing needed.

promptText: How does Immer's `produce(base, recipe)` let you write code that looks like direct mutation while actually producing a new immutable value with structural sharing?
options: It deep-clones the entire base object upfront, then lets you mutate the clone freely

It wraps the base in a Proxy "draft"; the set trap records which paths were written to and performs copy-on-write only for those paths and their ancestors, while any untouched subtree is returned by reference unchanged
It serializes the base to JSON and re-parses it after the recipe runs
It relies entirely on Object.freeze to prevent any actual mutation from occurring
explanation: Immer wraps the base object in a Proxy; reads are forwarded (with nested objects lazily wrapped too), and writes trigger copy-on-write for exactly the modified path up to the root — branches the recipe never touched are returned by the original reference, which is what preserves referential equality for unchanged subtrees.
